detail.longDescription:
So, I did something silly. Several silly things, really. It’s so silly that I’m a little afraid to share, because many of y’all are Actual Professional Programmers™ who have been doing it for decades and I’m one step removed from being a total newbie. My code quality, and the choices I made reflected therein, are probably not great.

But hey, I’m learning. It’s part of the process, right?

Long story short, I wrote the same program four times, in four languages (Windows batch file, bash script, C#, Swift), for three different platforms (Linux, macOS, Windows). I also wrote an entirely different cross-platform program in C++. I’m not a big fan of learning things by following a textbook in chapter order. Apparently, I prefer EXTREME PAIN and baptisms by fire.

The first program (the one I wrote four times) is OneDrive CLI control. Yeah, OneDrive. I would love to migrate to something else, but I have yet to find an alternative that works on Linux, macOS, and Windows that isn’t Dropbox (which doesn’t feel like much of an improvement, and is also more expensive to boot). Anyway, I store my development projects on OneDrive, and I’ll be the first to acknowledge that this is not a great idea. But at least I have the good sense to quit OneDrive before working on my projects, to prevent nasty sync errors.

On macOS and Windows, I could quit OneDrive the normal way via the menu bar or system tray respectively. On Linux, I could just run `systemctl --user stop onedrive`. But I guess that wasn’t good enough for me. I wanted an fast and easy way of doing it without leaving my terminal emulator, and Microsoft inexplicably doesn’t ship their own solution. (Yet?) So I wrote my own. Multiple times.

Linux was simple. It’s just a bash script that provides shorter aliases for `systemctl` commands. For example, the aforementioned stop command is reduced to `odctl stop`. It was laughably easy, and the script is less than 60 lines long.

https://github.com/digichelle/odctl-linux
